title: A function as a set of pairs
objectives: Treat a function as a set of input and output pairs with a domain and a codomain.

screens.title: Who sits where
screens.prose: Three traders and four desks. Each cell pairs a trader with a desk. Ana sits on FX, Ben on Rates and Cal on FX.
screens.question: Shade the cell for each trader's desk.

hints.text: Work one row at a time: one trader per row.
Ana's row: the FX column.
Ana–FX, Ben–Rates and Cal–FX: one cell in each row.

feedback.correct: Right. One cell in each row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shade the one cell in each row that matches the seating.

byKey.fx-taken: You left Cal without a desk. Two traders may share FX; Cal sits there too.
byKey.cal-moved: You moved Cal to Equities, perhaps because FX was taken. Cal sits on FX with Ana.
byKey.r1c1: Ana sits on FX, not Rates.
byKey.r2c2: Ben sits on Rates, not FX.

explain.text: Each trader sits on exactly one desk, so each row has exactly one shaded cell. Ana and Cal share FX, and that is allowed. Equities and Credit have nobody.

screens.title: Ordered pairs
screens.prose: Each cell is an **ordered pair**, such as $(\text{Ana}, \text{FX})$. Order matters: $(\text{Ana}, \text{FX}) \ne (\text{FX}, \text{Ana})$, though $\{\text{Ana}, \text{FX}\} = \{\text{FX}, \text{Ana}\}$. All the cells make up $A \times B$, every (trader, desk) pair.
screens.question: How many elements has $A \times B$?

hints.text: Each cell of the grid is one pair.
3 rows and 4 columns.
$|A \times B| = 3 \times 4 = 12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every cell, shaded or not.

byKey.added: You added $3 + 4$. Each trader pairs with each of the 4 desks, so multiply.
byKey.shaded: You counted the shaded cells. $A \times B$ is every cell.

explain.text: Each of the 3 traders pairs with each of the 4 desks. So $|A \times B| = 3 \times 4 = 12$, one pair per cell.

screens.title: Two desks
screens.prose: Any set of cells is a **relation** from $A$ to $B$. A relation is a **function** $f : A \to B$ when each row has exactly one cell. Here Ana is shaded on FX and on Credit.
screens.question: Is this relation a function from $A$ to $B$?

options.text: No. Ana's row has two cells
Yes. Every trader has a desk
options.why: You checked “at least one desk”. A function needs exactly one per trader, and Ana has two.

options.text: No. Nobody sits on Equities
options.why: An empty column is allowed. The rule counts cells per row, not per column.

options.text: No. Ana and Cal share FX
options.why: Sharing a desk is allowed. Two rows may use the same column.

hints.text: Count the shaded cells in each row.
Look at Ana's row.
Ana's row has two cells, FX and Credit, so “exactly one” fails.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells in each row.

byKey.yes: You accepted two desks for Ana. Then $f(\text{Ana})$ has no single value.

explain.text: A function gives each input exactly one output. Ana's row has two cells, so $f(\text{Ana})$ is not defined as one desk. The relation is not a function.

screens.title: No desk
screens.prose: Now Cal has no desk at all: Cal's row is empty.
screens.question: Tap one cell that would make this relation a function.

hints.text: Which row breaks “exactly one cell per row”?
Cal's row needs a cell.
Any one cell in Cal's row works: Cal can sit on any desk.

feedback.correct: Right. Any desk for Cal gives each row exactly one cell.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the row with no cell and give it one.

byKey.r1c1: Ana already has a desk. A second one would break the rule for Ana.
byKey.r1c3: Ana already has a desk. A second one would break the rule for Ana.
byKey.r1c4: Ana already has a desk. A second one would break the rule for Ana.
byKey.r2c2: Ben already has a desk. A second one would break the rule for Ben.
byKey.too-many: One cell is enough. Two in Cal's row would break the rule again.

explain.text: An empty row means an input with no output, so $f(\text{Cal})$ is undefined. One cell in Cal's row fixes it, whichever desk. Any of the four choices gives a function.

screens.title: Arrows
screens.prose: The same function as an **arrow diagram**: an arrow from each trader to their desk. $f(\text{Ana}) = \text{FX}$, $f(\text{Ben}) = \text{Rates}$ and $f(\text{Cal}) = \text{FX}$.

state.caption: Traders in $A$ on the left, desks in $B$ on the right

screens.question: Drop each trader's desk into their slot. Each drop draws an arrow.

Ana: FX. Ben: Rates. Cal: FX.

byKey.t-eq: Nobody sits on Equities. Cal sits on FX, with Ana.

explain.text: In an arrow diagram, a function has exactly one arrow leaving each input. Two arrows may land on the same output, as at FX. The grid and the arrows show the same set of pairs.

screens.title: The arrow that breaks it
screens.prose: Another relation from traders to desks, drawn as arrows.

state.caption: Traders in $A$ on the left, desks in $B$ on the right

screens.question: Tap one arrow you could remove to make this a function.

Ben has two arrows.
Remove either of Ben's arrows. Then each trader has exactly one.

feedback.correct: Right. Then exactly one arrow leaves each trader.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the trader with two arrows leaving.

byKey.e-cal-eq: Cal has only one arrow. Removing it leaves Cal with no desk.

screens.title: How many functions
screens.prose: A function from $A$ to $B$ picks one desk for Ana, one for Ben and one for Cal. Any desk is allowed each time.

state.caption: Traders in $A$ on the left, desks in $B$ on the right

screens.question: How many functions are there from $A$ to $B$?

hints.text: How many choices has Ana? Ben? Cal?
Each trader has 4 desks to choose from, independently.
$4 \times 4 \times 4 = 4^3 = 64$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of choices for each trader.

byKey.pairs: You counted the pairs, $3 \times 4$. A function is a choice of one pair per trader.
byKey.swap: You computed $3^4$: three choices for each desk. It is four choices for each trader.
byKey.inj: You stopped traders sharing a desk. Sharing is allowed, so Ben still has 4 choices.

explain.text: Ana has 4 choices, then Ben has 4 and Cal has 4, since desks may be shared. So there are $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$ functions. In general there are $|B|^{|A|}$ functions from $A$ to $B$.

screens.title: Everyone on FX
screens.prose: A reorganisation puts every trader on FX. The grid shows the new relation.
screens.question: Is this relation a function from $A$ to $B$?

options.text: Yes. Each row has exactly one cell
No. Rates, Equities and Credit are unused
options.why: You added a rule that every desk must be used. A function only needs one cell in each row.

options.text: No. Different traders must sit on different desks
options.why: You added a rule that outputs must differ. A function allows inputs to share an output.

options.text: No. A function cannot give the same output every time
options.why: A constant function is still a function, like $h(x) = 7$ in Functions.

hints.text: Apply the definition, row by row, and nothing more.
Each row has one cell, in the FX column.
Exactly one cell per row, so it is a function. Its outputs are all FX.

feedback.correct: Right. It is a function, with image $\{\text{FX}\}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check only the rule: exactly one cell in each row.

byKey.onto: You required every desk to be used. That is a different property, onto, which comes next lesson.
byKey.share: You required different outputs. That is one-to-one, a different property. A function may send many inputs to one output.

explain.text: Each trader has exactly one desk, so this is a function. Unused desks and a shared desk break no rule. The set of outputs actually reached is $\{\text{FX}\}$.

screens.title: A function is a set
screens.prose: A function $f : A \to B$ is a set of pairs $f \subseteq A \times B$ with exactly one pair for each element of $A$. $A$ is the **domain** and $B$ the **codomain**, the declared target. The **image** is $\{f(a) : a \in A\}$, the outputs actually reached; Functions called it the range.
screens.question: What is the image of the seating function $f$ shown?

options.text: $\{\text{FX}, \text{Rates}\}$
$\{\text{Rates}, \text{FX}, \text{Equities}, \text{Credit}\}$
options.why: You gave the codomain. The image holds only the desks someone sits on.

options.text: $\{\text{Ana}, \text{Ben}, \text{Cal}\}$
options.why: You gave the domain, the inputs. The image is a set of outputs.

options.text: $\{\text{FX}, \text{FX}, \text{Rates}\}$ with 3 elements
options.why: You counted FX twice. As a set it is $\{\text{FX}, \text{Rates}\}$, with 2 elements.

feedback.correct: Right. FX and Rates are reached; Equities and Credit are not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the outputs that some trader actually has.

explain.text: The shaded cells sit in the FX and Rates columns. So the image is $\{\text{FX}, \text{Rates}\}$, smaller than the codomain $B$. The codomain can be bigger than the image.

screens.title: Same rule, different function
screens.prose: Two functions follow the rule “square the input”. Functions are equal when they have the same domain, the same codomain and the same pairs.
screens.question: Are $f$ and $g$ the same function?

options.text: No. Their domains differ, so their sets of pairs differ
Yes. They have the same rule
options.why: You compared rules only. $(0.5, 0.25)$ is a pair of $g$ but not of $f$.

options.text: Yes. They agree on every integer
options.why: They agree where both are defined, but $g$ has pairs $f$ lacks, such as $(0.5, 0.25)$.

options.text: No. Only $g$ can output 4
options.why: Both output 4: $f(2) = g(2) = 4$. The difference is in the domains.

hints.text: Compare the sets of pairs, not just the rules.
Is $(0.5, 0.25)$ a pair of $f$?
0.5 is not an integer, so $(0.5, 0.25) \in g$ but $\notin f$. The functions differ.

feedback.correct: Right. Same rule, different domains, different functions.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List one pair that is in one function but not the other.

byKey.rule: You let the rule decide. A function is its domain, codomain and pairs, and the domains differ.

explain.text: $g$ contains $(0.5, 0.25)$ and $f$ does not, since $0.5 \notin \mathbb{Z}$. So the sets of pairs differ and $f \ne g$. The graph of $g$ is the set $\{(x, x^2) : x \in \mathbb{R}\}$, a curve in the plane.

screens.title: Which mappings are functions
screens.prose: A risk system keeps several lookups. A sample of the first:
screens.question: Which are functions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ticker to sector: each ticker has one sector
Trade id to trade record, in a table keyed by trade id
Sector to ticker
options.why: You read the table backwards. Banks goes to BARC and to LLOY, so one input has two outputs.

options.text: Trader to the trades they booked today
options.why: A trader may book several trades, or none. Then one input has many outputs, or none.

hints.text: For each mapping, ask: does every input have exactly one output?
Banks has two tickers in the sample.
Ticker to sector and trade id to record are functions. Sector to ticker and trader to trades are not.

feedback.correct: Right. A key column is what makes a lookup a function.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each mapping for exactly one output per input.

byKey.sector: You picked sector to ticker. Banks maps to both BARC and LLOY.
byKey.trader: You picked trader to trades. A busy trader has many, a quiet one none.
byKey.tick: You left out ticker to sector. Each ticker belongs to one sector, though sectors are shared.
byKey.id: You left out the trade-id table. A key gives each id exactly one record.

explain.text: Each ticker has one sector, and sharing a sector is allowed. A table keyed by trade id gives each id exactly one record. Banks maps to two tickers, so the reverse lookup is not a function.

ideas: $A \times B$ is the set of ordered pairs $(a, b)$, and $|A \times B| = |A| \times |B|$. A relation is any subset of it.
A function $f : A \to B$ is a relation with exactly one pair for each $a \in A$. Shared outputs and unused outputs are allowed.
The domain and codomain are part of the function; the image is the outputs reached. There are $|B|^{|A|}$ functions from $A$ to $B$.

formula.name: Function
formula.tex: \forall a \in A\ \exists \text{ exactly one } b \in B : (a, b) \in f
formula.note: One cell in every row of the $A \times B$ grid.

summary.trap: A function need not use every output, and two inputs may share one. Everyone on FX is a function.

quiz.prose: $\varnothing \times B = \varnothing$, since there are no first entries. $B$ is the four desks.
quiz.question: How many functions are there from $\varnothing$ to $B$?

feedback.correct: Right. One: the empty set of pairs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which subsets of $\varnothing \times B$ have one pair per element of $\varnothing$.

byKey.zero: You looked for pairs. The empty set of pairs has one pair for each element of $\varnothing$, vacuously, so it is a function.
byKey.four: You gave one function per desk. With no inputs there is nothing to send anywhere.

explain.text: The only subset of $\varnothing \times B$ is $\varnothing$. Its condition, one pair per element of the domain, holds vacuously. So there is exactly one function, the empty function, and $4^0 = 1$ agrees.

options.why: That is the codomain. $c$ is never reached.
That is the domain.

options.why: Sharing an output is allowed. Each input has exactly one output.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Collect the second entries of the pairs.

explain.text: The second entries are $a$, $a$ and $b$. As a set that is $\{a, b\}$. The codomain $\{a, b, c\}$ is bigger.
